lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 10–12 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Fall of the House of Usher.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Fall of the House of Usher: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

lessonPlan.middleSchoolTrack: Short story: read whole in one 90-minute lesson (assign longer stories as pre-reading). Middle School prompts use the full text when the grade tags include 6–8; otherwise teacher-selected passages.
lessonPlan.schedule: One 90-minute lesson (the whole story), with an optional take-home essay
essentialQuestions: What does The Fall of the House of Usher suggest about decay of family and mind?

objectives: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly and implicitly.
Determine themes and analyze their development over the course of the story.
Analyze how characters, setting and point of view interact.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.

wholeBookTest.title: The Fall of the House of Usher: whole-book test

items.prompt: Why does the narrator visit the House of Usher?
options: He is lost in a storm
He wants to buy it
Roderick wrote asking for his company
He is a doctor called to Madeline

items.prompt: What flaw does the narrator notice in the house's front?
options: A barely visible crack running down the wall
A missing door
A broken window
A fallen tower
The housekeeper
Roderick's wife
The narrator's cousin
Roderick's twin sister

items.prompt: What happens to Madeline that turns out to be terrible?
options: She marries the narrator
She is entombed while still alive
She runs away
She burns the house

items.prompt: What happens to the house at the end?
options: It splits apart and sinks into the tarn
The narrator inherits it
It burns down
It is sold

items.prompt: In the line “I regarded her with an utter astonishment not unmingled with dread—and yet I found it impossible to account for such feelings.”, what does “unmingled” most nearly mean?
options: to increase
provide physical relief, as from pain
pure; not mixed with anything else
open to two or more interpretations; or of uncertain nature or significance; or (often) intended to mislead

items.prompt: In the line “For several days ensuing, her name was unmentioned by either Usher or myself; and during this period I was busied in earnest endeavors to alleviate the melancholy of my friend.”, what does “alleviate” most nearly mean?
options: to increase
provide physical relief, as from pain
pure; not mixed with anything else
open to two or more interpretations; or of uncertain nature or significance; or (often) intended to mislead

items.prompt: As used in the story (“I regarded her with an utter astonishment not unmingled with dread—and yet I found it impossible to account for such feelings.”), what does “unmingled” mean?
options: pure; not mixed with anything else
abandon hope; give up hope; lose heart
have some of the qualities or attributes of something
provide physical relief, as from pain

items.prompt: As used in the story (“For several days ensuing, her name was unmentioned by either Usher or myself; and during this period I was busied in earnest endeavors to al”), what does “alleviate” mean?
options: a feeling of alarm or dread
provide physical relief, as from pain
a careful reading
to increase

items.prompt: As used in the story (“Much that I encountered on the way contributed, I know not how, to heighten the vague sentiments of which I have already spoken.”), what does “heighten” mean?
options: produced or growing in extreme abundance
explained point by point
to increase

items.prompt: As used in the story (“I learned, moreover, at intervals, and through broken and equivocal hints, another singular feature of his mental condition.”), what does “equivocal” mean?
options: have some of the qualities or attributes of something

shortAnswer: Explain how decay of family and mind develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how fear and the imagination develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.

wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the story's central concerns (decay of family and mind, fear and the imagination, the double) and argue how the ending reframes it.

essayAssignments.title: Essay: Decay of family and mind

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what The Fall of the House of Usher teaches about decay of family and mind. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Edgar Allan Poe develops decay of family and mind in The Fall of the House of Usher. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Edgar Allan Poe develops decay of family and mind across The Fall of the House of Usher. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of The Fall of the House of Usher (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of decay of family and mind. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of decay of family and mind in The Fall of the House of Usher. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Edgar Allan Poe's choices in The Fall of the House of Usher (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of decay of family and mind, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places The Fall of the House of Usher's treatment of decay of family and mind in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on decay of family and mind in The Fall of the House of Usher that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on decay of family and mind in The Fall of the House of Usher. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about decay of family and mind in The Fall of the House of Usher, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on decay of family and mind in The Fall of the House of Usher, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
